title: Operating Distributed Inference Systems at Scale — Nishant Gupta & Naman Ahuja, Meta
talk_summary: Meta infra engineers describe inference serving as a distributed-systems control-plane problem: routing, caching, batching, admission control, and reliability must be coordinated, and the right metric is cost per successful task, not cost per token. They give a four-quadrant optimization framework (avoid/share/move/delay work) and warn about cascading failures and retry amplification.

takeaways.technique: Optimize cost per successful task, not per token/request
takeaways.what_they_do: They define the KPI as cost per successful task, folding in retries, storage, failures, network, and ops cost, because that is what users actually care about.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We have to optimize cost per successful task because this is what actually users care about.
Can we avoid the work? ... Can we share the work? ... Can we move away the work? ... Can we delay the work?

takeaways.what_they_do: The scheduler knows a request is step 3 of 5 and how much has already been spent, so it can prioritize, admit, or terminate workflows to avoid wasting prior compute.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If a step three fails the whole workflow will be terminated and we have wasted all that compute resources.

takeaways.technique: Circuit breakers, load shedding on queue depth, retry budgets
takeaways.what_they_do: They design deliberate circuit breakers at routing, admission control that rejects rather than queues, load shedding tied to queue depth (not CPU/memory), and retry budgets to prevent retry-amplified cascades.

takeaways.technique: Control plane owns reliability, not the edge
takeaways.what_they_do: Because partial failures mid-stream are hard to retry at the edge, reliability is made a property of the control plane that sees the whole workflow.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Reliability we cannot build reliability at the edge. It has to be a property of the control plane.

takeaways.technique: Observability as control-loop input (TTFT, utilization, success-per-dollar, end-to-end latency)
takeaways.what_they_do: They treat telemetry as the input signal to scheduling/routing decisions, tracking time-to-first-token, utilization ratio, success per dollar, and end-to-end latency, then feeding changes back into the control loop.
